strengths: Provides a mathematically rigorous, closed-form derivation for ray-Gaussian transmittance that removes the linear/projective (EWA/UT) approximation error inherent to splatting-based 3DGS variants, with a clean canonical-coordinate proof (Theorem 1) and full gradient derivations in the appendix.

Introduces Particle Bounding Frustum (PBF) association, an efficient closed-form (quadratic-equation) alternative to BVH traversal or Unscented-Transform-based conic approximation; empirically shown to yield 2.5-5x fewer Gaussians per tile and clear runtime gains over EWA/UT association (Tab. K.5, K.6).

Proposes the Bipolar Equiangular Projection (BEAP), a camera-agnostic image parameterization that unifies pinhole/fisheye supervision and yields more uniform angular ray sampling, with a dedicated ablation (Sec. 4.5, Table 6) showing consistent gains over perspective/equidistant supervision.

Extensive empirical validation spanning four datasets (ScanNet++, ZipNeRF, Aria, MipNeRF360) with both fisheye and pinhole cameras, including cross-camera generalization (fisheye-to-pinhole and vice versa), extreme/out-of-distribution FoV generalization, and central-vs-peripheral region analysis -- all supporting the central claim of reduced approximation error under wide FoV.

Careful ablations isolate the contribution of each component: transmittance formulation vs. splatting approximation (Sec 4.4, Fig 8), association strategy (Table K.6), and BEAP supervision (Table 6), plus a Gaussian-count scaling study (Fig. 5) directly rebutting a concurrent claim (Celarek et al. 2025) that brute-force scaling closes the approximation gap.

Thorough appendix with full derivations, numerical-stability discussion (including a concrete demonstration of a competing method's instability, Fig. C.1), algorithmic pseudocode, and a discussion contextualizing the method relative to 2DGS/HTGS and prior ray-tracing methods (3DGRT/3DGUT/EVER).

Runtime comparable to or approaching optimized 3DGS splatting (Table 4, Table K.4) while retaining exactness, and about 5x faster than prior projective-exact ray-based baselines, which is a meaningful systems contribution beyond the geometric derivation.
weaknesses: The title/abstract claim of rendering being made fully 'exact' is somewhat overstated; Appendix A explicitly admits the method still relies on maximum-response/ordering approximations and does not resolve self-occlusion or overlapping attenuation exactly, which should be more prominently flagged in the main text rather than relegated to a limitations appendix.

The mirror-transformation trick (Sec D.2, with heuristic parameter ξ=1 fixed across all experiments) used to handle PBF-CSF intersection outside the monotonic tan domain is somewhat ad hoc; sensitivity of results to this hyperparameter, and behavior at or near 180° circular FoV boundaries, is not analyzed.

The method introduces substantial additional complexity (canonical transforms, PBF quadratic solves, mirror angle bookkeeping, BEAP inverse interpolation) relative to 3DGS; although runtime is competitive, the implementation/engineering burden and reproducibility risk are nontrivially higher, and code is only promised, not yet available for review.

Evaluation is centered on indoor/bounded or moderate-scale scenes (ScanNet++, Aria, MipNeRF360 objects); there is limited evidence of behavior on very large-scale outdoor/unbounded scenes or highly dynamic content, where ordering/self-occlusion approximations (acknowledged as a limitation) may matter more.

The paper reports an extremely large number of tables/ablations (K.1-K.9) which, while thorough, makes it hard to discern which comparisons are most central; some presentation streamlining between main text and appendix could improve clarity.

All baselines appear to be self-reimplemented/reproduced by the authors (with some numbers sourced from original papers only for the FPS metric), so there is some risk of reproduction bias favoring the proposed method, though this is common practice in the field.
